EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across the state.  Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 1%, D2 - 54%, D1 - 55%.  January  brought little relief to Maine's drought conditions, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge.  January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas in the 50 to 75% of normal range.  Snowfall remained below normal, especially for interior areas with snow water equivalent below normal for all areas except the immediate coast.  Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins.  Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the immediate coastline in the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought conditions remained in a steady state by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Snow overspread the Casco Bay area by the afternoon on the 25th. Within an hour or two snow was moderate to heavy at times as an intense band of lift moved into the region. Snowfall rates were one to two inches per hour during the heavy snow. Snow continued overnight into the 26th, with occasional breaks or lighter snowfall before the storm center moved into the Atlantic. Snowfall totals ranged from 12 to 16 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: An expansive winter storm gripped much of the country beginning on the 24th. An anomalously cold air mass was in place ahead of the storm, which tracked through the southern Plains and across the Southeast. A significant cold air dam remained in place east of the Appalachian Mountains and helped to force secondary cyclogenesis south of New England on the 25th. Strong warm air advection in the mid levels forced an intense band of snow that lifted north through New England, reaching New Hampshire and western Maine during the afternoon. Snow quickly became moderate to heavy after onset. Snowfall rates were at times one inch or more per hour as the band lifted northward. In its wake lower level forcing continued the moderate to heavy snow near the Massachusetts border through the overnight into the morning of the 26th. This resulted in the highest snowfall totals across southeast New Hampshire and southwestern Maine. The upper level trough swung through the region on the 26th with light snow for much of the day, ending as one final burst of moderate snow in the evening. Key message: heavy snow, traffic accidents.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: At the start of 2026, drought conditions were widespread across the state.  Drought conditions as Percent Area of the state: D3 - 1%, D2 - 54%, D1 - 55%.  January  brought little relief to Maine's drought conditions, as winter set in and frozen ground effectively halted any potential for significant groundwater recharge.  January precipitation remained below to well below normal with most areas in the 50 to 75% of normal range.  Snowfall remained below normal, especially for interior areas with snow water equivalent below normal for all areas except the immediate coast.  Streamflow and ground water remained well below normal on all basins.  Dry well reports in January began to slacken off compared to previous months.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: January can be summarized by a frozen cap effect as well below normal temperatures and significant frost depths prevented any meaningful sub-surface water recharge.  In addition, precipitation remained below normal for the entire region for the month.  This led to a lower than normal snowpack for all areas except the immediate coastline in the month.  Overall, conditions in January didn't improve the drought and drought conditions remained in a steady state by the end of the month.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A weakening surface low crossed northern Maine during the 1st. At the same time...a secondary low developed across the Gulf of Maine and tracked toward Nova Scotia with a trof extending between the lows. Snow developed during the early morning hours of the 1st...persisting into the evening. A meso-scale snow band developed along the trof axis...running across central and coastal portions of Washington county. Localized snow fall rates of up to 4 inches per hour occurred with this band. The greatest storm total snow accumulation occurred with the band...with totals of 8 to 14 inches. Storm totals across Washington county...outside of this band...ranged from 5 to 8 inches. Warning criteria snow accumulations occurred during the late afternoon of the 1st. Storm total snow accumulations of 4 to 6 inches occurred to the north of Washington county across the remainder of eastern Maine along the trof axis. Snow totals tapered to 1 to 2 inches across western portions of the forecast area.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Overall drought conditions did not change across northern and eastern Maine during January. Several storms impacted the region during January bringing mostly snow, though a wintry mix and rain did occasionally occur across mostly Downeast areas. The heaviest snows generally occurred across east-central and Downeast portions of the region. Monthly precipitation totals for January generally ranged from 0.50 to 1.50 inches below normal across northern and eastern Maine. However...with frozen ground preventing soil penetration...soil moisture and groundwater was relatively unchanged during the month. Severe ( D2 ) level drought conditions generally remained unchanged from late December. Moderate ( D1 ) level drought conditions persisted across the remainder of the region.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Overall Severe ( D2 ) level drought conditions persisted through January...unchanged from late December.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Despite the seasonal transition, Maine remained locked in drought. Persistent precipitation deficits over the winter, falling as low as 50% of normal in southern areas during March, prevented categorical recovery. As of late March, 53% of Maine were classified under D2 (Severe Drought) conditions. Portions of coastal Maine continued to experience D3 (Extreme Drought). During March 2026, drought conditions across Maine experienced subtle seasonal shifts but largely maintained their designations from the U.S. Drought Monitor (USDM). Sizable long-term deficits persisted despite variable precipitation across northern and eastern sectors. Ground conditions began a slow transition as warmer periods mid-month started breaking thaw topsoil layers, allowing localized infiltration. Precipitation across the southern and western counties remained below normal, maintaining hydrologic stress on regional aquifers and private wells.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Waldo County averaged 3.08 inches of precipitation in March, approximately 0.89 inches below normal, marking the third driest start to the new year, and the driest June through March stretch on record. The USDM on March 31st had 100% of the county in Severe Drought (D2).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into March in northern and coastal Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure tracks east over New England, and south of the Gulf of Maine on Sunday evening. Warm front with associated low pressure stays over the Maine gulf  Sunday evening into night. Snow moves in Sunday morning and continues into Sunday evening. EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 6-8 inches of snow fell in Northern Somerset Sunday into Sunday evening. Isolated higher amounts in elevated areas, with a report from St. Aurelie Crossing of roughly 10 inches of snowfall.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Occluding low pressure system to the north moves east, further into Canada. Associated warm front moved through the state Tuesday evening, March 31st, and associated cold front moved through Maine quickly behind it on Wednesday, April 1st. Downeast region saw some snowfall early Tuesday morning, and alongside the warm front, mid-level warm air advection created a prime environment for some sleet development. Precipitation began as snow in the north, freezing rain/sleet in the Central Highlands, and rain Downeast. As the cold front quickly swept through the region, tanking temperatures. and resulting in more mixed precipitation. By the time the system fully moved through the region by Wednesday, roughly, 1/2 to just under 1 inch of sleet fell in Aroostook county. Roughly 0.1 to 0.25 inches of freezing rain fell in southern Aroostook, Piscataquis and northern Penobscot counties. Event continues into April 1st. System resulted in messy travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 2-3 inches of snowfall fell during the evening of the 31st. Frenchville ASOS reported a trace of freezing rain by April 1st.

Downeast region saw some snowfall early Tuesday morning, and alongside the warm front, mid-level warm air advection created a prime environment for some sleet development. Precipitation began as snow in the north, freezing rain/sleet in the Central Highlands, and rain Downeast. As the cold front quickly swept through the region, tanking temperatures. and resulting in more mixed precipitation. By the time the system fully moved through the region by Wednesday, roughly, 1/2 to just under 1 inch of sleet fell in Aroostook county. Roughly 0.1 to 0.25 inches of freezing rain fell in southern Aroostook, Piscataquis and northern Penobscot counties. Event continues into April 1st. System resulted in messy travel conditions.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-2 inches of snowfall and sleet fell during the evening of the 31st. Frenchville ASOS reported a trace of freezing rain by April 1st.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system moves northeast towards Maine on Wednesday, as an occluded front passes over the state on Thursday.  High pressure builds over Canada Wednesday, surging cold air into northern and eastern Maine. Cold air at the surface, plus plenty of warm air aloft, led to significant mixed precipitation accumulations mid-afternoon on Wednesday, through Thursday morning. Precipitation began as snow Wednesday morning in the north, a freezing rain/sleet mix in central regions, and rain Downeast. Snow in the north transitions generally over to sleet by Wednesday afternoon. Wednesday night, freezing rain fell south to north. Roughly 2 to 3 inches of sleet in the St. John Valley, North Woods, and Aroostook regions. Around 0.5 to 0.25 of an inch in Aroostook county, and 0.25 to 0.50 in Penobscot region. Roughly 2-4 inches of snow in the north.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Roughly 1-2 inches of sleet fell Wednesday into Wednesday evening in Northern Somerset.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system with an occluded front move to the northeast of Maine, bringing gusty winds and heavy rainfall to northern and eastern Maine. Rainfall resulted in significant snowmelt for remaining snow pack, and with a deep frost depth still in place over most of the state, majority of rainfall acted as runoff. Runoff and additional river ice melt led to ice jamming along the Piscataquis River, near North Howland and Maxfield roads. There were large ice chunks moving onto local property from this ice jam. Flooding began on Wednesdya, March 18th, and continued into Thursday, March 19th. Penobscot EMs evacuated impacted home, and set up shelters for those impacted.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: An ice jam on the Piscataquis River led to flooding which impacted portions of Maxfield and North Howland roads. These road was temporarily closed due to the flooding. Water levels fell that by Thursday afternoon.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Persistent drought continued into February in northern and central Maine. The ground was frozen the entire month in northern counties, continuing to restrict any moisture from penetrating down into the soil. Frost depth at the beginning of February was 21 inches at the Caribou office, gradually increasing to 26 inches by February 24th. All climate sites recorded below average precipitation, with generally 1.5 - 2.0 inch deficits. At the end of January, northern Somerset, northwestern Aroostook, northern Piscataquis, southern Penobscot, and central and coastal Hancock counties, were included in severe drought. The Central Highlands region, eastern and southern Aroostook, far northern Hancock, and Washington counties were in moderate drought. In February,  drought conditions remained status quo. No additional dry drinking well reports during February.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: A lack of adequate precipitation in Northwest Aroostook led to prolonged drying conditions in February. Conditions were Severe Drought (D2) in late January and stayed in Severe Drought to the end of the month. Drought continued into March.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure system from the west moved over Maine, late on 02/10 into 02/11. Occluded front moves over the state, bringing precipitation in the form of snow from west to southeast. Low began to slow down over eastern Maine, and alongside a surface low developing, heaviest snowfall occurred over eastern Maine. Warning criteria snowfall occurred in central and costal Washington county, with accumulations around 7-9 inches during the afternoon of the 11th. Storm total accumulations around 6-8 inches in southern Aroostook. Northern and eastern Aroostook, alongside Hancock county, had accumulations around 3-5 inches. The rest of the Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, and Bangor region received about 2-4 inches.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 4 to 7 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: On February 23rd, strong Nor'easter system moved northeast in the Atlantic, east of Cape Cod. It moved northeast through the Gulf of Maine, just south of Nova Scotia. Strong winds and plenty of moisture resulted in blizzard conditions in coastal Hancock, and central and coastal Washington county. Blizzard conditions verified during the afternoon of the 23rd in these areas. Heavy snow fell during the morning into the evening of the 23rd for northern Hancock county, with totals roughly 4 - 8 inches. Bangor region roughly got 1 - 5 inches of snow. Central Highlands, Upper Penobscot Valley, southern and eastern Aroostook county had accumulations around 1-2 inches. North Woods region only accumulated about a trace - 1 inch of snow. High winds results in isolated power outages, predominantly in Hancock county. Multiple school closures in Downeast region. Low pressure moved east of Maine by nighttime, with precipitation gradually slowing down.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 1 to 4 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Throughout February 2026, drought conditions in Maine remained stable in their classification from the USDM, maintaining extreme to severe drought conditions. By the end of the month, Maine���s drought coverage was nearly 1% Extreme Drought (D3), 53% Severe Drought (D2), and 46% Moderate Drought (D1). The freeze cap locked down any recharge to the system groundwater, while surface hydrologic conditions showed signs of continued deterioration with below normal precipitation. Precipitation during February was notably insufficient, with much of the region recording less than 50% of normal accumulations. This deficit was compounded by deep soil frost depths ranging from 6 to 20 inches, which acted as an impermeable barrier and prevented any melting snow or rain from recharging stressed aquifers. Consequently, groundwater levels in southern Maine continued to decline, reaching or falling below the historic lows observed during the 2002 drought. While snow was present across the state, the snowpack remained below normal in central and northern regions, and hundreds of households reported dry private wells due to the persistent lack of recovery.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Franklin County averaged 1.68 inches of precipitation in February, approximately 2.02 inches below normal, marking it the 3rd driest February. The USDM on February 24th had 85% of the county in Severe Drought (D2) and 15% in Extreme Drought (D3).

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began to develop over the Southeast on the morning of the 22nd. By the evening it had moved to a position off the Carolinas and was deepening rapidly. Between 7 pm on the 22nd and 7 am on the 23rd, central pressure in the storm dropped from 991 mb to 966 mb. The intense low pressure combined with high pressure around 1045 mb building into Quebec to produce a strong pressure gradient across the region. The result was strong wind gusts through much of the day on the 23rd. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the moderate snow did move into southwestern Maine. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. Key Messages: blizzard conditions, strong wind gusts, dangerous travel, traffic accidents.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Accumulating snow did not begin until around 7 am on the 23rd, but winds had already become gusty around midnight. As a result visibility was quickly reduced to 1/2 mile or less shortly after the snow started falling. During the mid morning into the early afternoon the Portland International Jetport observed blizzard conditions for nearly 5 straight hours. A peak wind gust of 56 mph was observed at 1156 am. The heavy snow never quite reached the Casco Bay area, and snowfall totals ranged from 3 to 6 inches.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Low pressure began to develop over the Southeast on the morning of the 22nd. By the evening it had moved to a position off the Carolinas and was deepening rapidly. Between 7 pm on the 22nd and 7 am on the 23rd, central pressure in the storm dropped from 991 mb to 966 mb. The intense low pressure combined with high pressure around 1045 mb building into Quebec to produce a strong pressure gradient across the region. The result was strong wind gusts through much of the day on the 23rd. While the heaviest snowfall remained largely over southern New England, the edge of the moderate snow did move into southwestern Maine. The combination of the two produced blizzard conditions and near-zero visibility at times. While winds continued to gust into the evening, snowfall tapered off in the late afternoon hours on the 23rd. Key Messages: blizzard conditions, strong wind gusts, dangerous travel, traffic accidents.

As a result visibility was quickly reduced to 1/2 mile or less shortly after the snow started falling. During the mid morning into the early afternoon the neighboring Portland International Jetport and Portsmouth International Airport at Pease observed blizzard conditions for nearly 5 straight hours. The heavy snow only reached the Kittery area, with snowfall totals ranging from 3 to 9 inches.
